rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid missing late compounds. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, spread across the gradient, or still retained into the high-organic hold.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so now optimize time aggressively. The first run suggests the elution window is much narrower than 0.05-0.95, so raise phi0, lower phi1, shorten tG, and raise T to pull the last peak closer to 10 min while checking that no pair collapses.

We already have the maximum CRF, so use the extra budget to probe the speed limit by shortening the gradient one step while keeping the same phi window and temperature. If resolution remains acceptable, this identifies whether the current method has unnecessary margin; if not, injection 2 is confirmed as near-optimal.

Resolution is still comfortably above 1.5 after shortening to 8 min, so push one more step shorter on tG with the same window and temperature. This tests whether we can further reduce run time before the early critical pair (1,2) falls too close.

The 6 min gradient still has a healthy minimum resolution, so continue stepping down tG to find the shortest method that keeps every adjacent pair at or above 1.5. Pair (1,2) is the emerging limiter, so this run should locate the edge more precisely.

At 4 min the limiting pair is still above the 1.5 threshold, so test the minimum allowed gradient time to see whether full-credit resolution can be maintained at the fastest possible method. This directly checks if the true optimum is the shortest grid point.

The 4 min method is fully resolving but pair 1/2 is the limiter, so lower phi0 one step to give the earliest pair more retention and spacing while keeping the run fast. This tests whether a slightly wider low-end window improves robustness without sacrificing the excellent time performance.

Lowering phi0 slightly preserved full resolution at 4 min, so now test whether that extra low-end retention is enough to rescue the critical 1/2 pair at the minimum 2 min gradient. If it succeeds, this would be the fastest possible fully scoring method on the grid.

Since 2 min cannot maintain the first pair, refine around the successful 4 min method by narrowing the high end one step. The last peak is far earlier than 10 min, so a slightly smaller phi1 may preserve full resolution while trimming unnecessary gradient range and testing robustness of the later peaks.

Narrowing to phi1 0.65 improved the limiting resolution at 4 min, so now retest the 2 min minimum gradient with this better-focused window. This is the most direct shot at finding a fully resolved method faster than the current 4 min gradients.

The 2 min run improved as phi1 was lowered from 0.70 to 0.65, so continue narrowing the gradient window at the high end to see if the critical first pair can be pushed to full resolution at the minimum tG. The 2 min gradient keeps improving as phi1 decreases, and the last peak is still well before 10 min, so push phi1 down one more step. This is the best remaining path to see whether the minimum-time method can still achieve full-credit resolution for the first pair.

The 2 min method is moving steadily toward full resolution as phi1 is lowered, and the last peak still remains under the 10 min limit. One more step down in phi1 tests whether the shortest possible gradient can finally bring the first pair to R >= 1.5 without incurring a time penalty.

Doubling tG should recover full resolution while likely keeping t_last under 10 min, potentially giving a faster fully robust 1.000 method than the earlier 4 min, phi1 0.65-0.70 runs.

The narrowed high end improves the difficult first pair but makes the last peak too late, so raise temperature to pull the tail back under 10 min while keeping the favorable phi window. The best fast methods all hinge on the first pair, and increasing temperature from 50 to 55 C slightly eroded that margin while shortening the run.
